summary:
A Q&A-format piece in Workplace Insight featuring St John Ambulance trainer Annick Bessawa on turning World Mental Health Day into year-round workplace wellbeing practice. The 2025 theme emphasised listening to people with lived experience (PWLE) of mental health conditions to build understanding and reduce stigma.

Key guidance offered:

Participation: employers should offer opportunities for everyone but keep involvement voluntary, since mental health is personal and some staff will not want to share. Activities should be varied, inclusive and accessible across personalities, generations and cultures, supporting psychological safety.

Engagement tactics: small-group creative activities work best because they are interactive and hands-on, and people open up more readily in small groups than large forums. Fun challenges or friendly competition with a reward increase participation.

Low or no budget options: use free World Health Organisation resources including fact sheets and video testimonials from people with lived experience. Teams can watch a short video then build a poster, or pick a condition fact sheet and present on causes, treatments and practical support.

Overlooked wellbeing activity: taking lunch away from the desk or going for a walk. Employers can encourage team lunches, welcoming communal spaces, occasional screen-free lunches where staff switch off from email and meetings, and lunchtime walking groups. These cost little but boost morale, relationships and belonging.

Disclosure handling: listen with empathy and without judgement, maintain confidentiality, thank the person for speaking up, avoid minimising concerns, and signpost to Employee Assistance Programmes, occupational health, mental health first aiders or external professionals. Managers are not expected to act as clinicians.

Sustaining impact beyond 10 October: treat the day as a catalyst, embed wellbeing in everyday culture through regular conversations, manager and mental health first aider training, promotion of support services, wellbeing check-ins, awareness campaigns, peer support networks, periodic wellbeing surveys, and encouraging regular breaks and annual leave.
